read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7 and Appendices B-F (dataset statistics, training hyperparameters, extra downstream results, AlphaGeometry soundness, comparison with LeanEuclid/LeanGeo/MATP); A (Lean header) and G (Aristotle proofs) skimmed

claims.claim: Competition geometry problems can be automatically translated into Lean 4 statements that use only standard mathlib (the plane as two-dimensional Euclidean space, no custom axioms or external solvers), at the scale of hundreds of thousands of problems, if a language model is made to state explicitly the non-degeneracy and configuration assumptions that informal geometry leaves implicit: retrieving mathlib definitions together with the side conditions each needs, sketching an informal proof first to commit to a configuration, and repairing statements from compiler errors. Supported only if at least 95% of problems in both a 780-problem olympiad set and a 184K-problem web-scale set get at least one compiling statement; if expert annotators judge the first of five compiling candidates faithful for at least 45% of 180 competition problems of difficulty 4 or above and at least one of the five faithful for at least 70%; and if, on a 30-problem ablation, adding concept mapping, compiler-feedback repair and constraint mapping each raises the compiling rate, while proof-first anchoring, though it slightly lowers compilation, wins more paired human faithfulness comparisons than it loses.
claims.decision_rule: Retention >= 95% (OMNI 98.5%, Numina 96.6%); human TOP1 >= 45%, TOP5 >= 70% (180 problems, difficulty >= 4); ablation compile counts increase 125 -> 254 -> 465 -> 500; anchoring 480 compiles but paired wins > losses (7 vs 3).
subfields_hint: LLM code generation with compiler feedback

claims.claim: Because the formalizations live in standard mathlib, general-purpose neural provers trained only on non-geometry mathlib problems already prove some of them, and training on the resulting proofs improves geometry proving further, including on held-out problems and for a second prover. Supported only if Goedel-Prover v2 (8B) with no geometry-specific training proves at least 13% of the 177,597-problem corpus at Pass@1; if one round of fine-tuning on its own successful proofs or preference pairs raises this by at least 1 point, with paired gains clearly outnumbering losses; if the trained models also improve on the held-out olympiad set; and if fine-tuning DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B the same way raises its Pass@1 by at least 1 point.
claims.decision_rule: Goedel v2 base Pass@1 >= 13% (13.6); SFT and DPO >= base + 1 (15.1, 15.0); paired gains/losses ~2:1; OMNI held-out Pass@1 up (6.90 -> 7.68/7.81); DeepSeek-Prover-V2 base + 1 (13.4 -> 15.0).

experiments.text: Define the pipeline and corpora. Setup: DeepSeek-V3 generates every stage: (1) constraint explication, e.g. 'D on segment BC' becomes strict betweenness Sbtw, 'triangle ABC' adds AffineIndependent, 'line AB' adds A != B, 'circle' adds r > 0, and point order on a circle becomes a cross-product sign; (2) an informal proof sketch first, to commit to one configuration; (3) retrieval of mathlib definitions with their required side conditions; (4) compile-and-repair using Lean error messages. 32 candidates per problem. OMNI-Geometry: 780 plane-geometry problems from OMNI-Math (difficulty 1-9.5, 557 from HMMT); Numina-Geometry: 183,796 NuminaMath problems labelled geometry (32.5% olympiads, 26.2% Chinese K-12, 17.8% synthetic), a subset the official NuminaMath-Lean release excluded as too hard to formalise.

Measure coverage and expert-judged faithfulness. Result: 768 of 780 (98.5%) and 177,597 of 183,796 (96.6%) problems have at least one compiling statement. Graduate annotators with Lean experience judge 180 random OMNI-Geometry problems of difficulty >= 4 (five compiling candidates each): TOP1 / TOP5 faithful 50.94 / 77.36% (difficulty 4-5, n = 53), 55.84 / 76.62% (5-6, n = 77), 43.75 / 75.00% (6-7, n = 16), 42.11 / 57.89% (7-8, n = 19), 20.00 / 60.00% (8+, n = 15); overall 48.89 / 73.33%.

Ablate the pipeline. Setup: 30 OMNI-Geometry problems, 32 samples each (960 candidates per configuration). Result: compiling candidates 125 (13.0%) with basic prompting, 254 (26.5%) adding concept mapping, 465 (48.4%) adding compiler-feedback repair, 500 (52.1%) adding constraint mapping, 480 (50.0%) adding proof-first anchoring. A paired human Pass@3 comparison of the last two: anchoring wins 7, loses 3, 10 both correct, 10 both wrong, which the authors read as better faithfulness because anchoring adds configuration constraints whose absence would not break compilation.

Note what compilation and coverage do not show. Setup: retention counts any compiling statement, and compilation is a weak proxy for meaning; on 100 random Numina-Geometry problems, the frontier prover Aristotle refutes some statements as false, finds others trivial through misformalization or with concrete counterexamples, proves 25 and leaves 19 unresolved but unrefuted (the number filtered is not stated). Corpus-scale semantic checking is not done; the authors call Numina-Geometry a candidate corpus and note that over-strong injected hypotheses can make statements easier or vacuous. Text only: problems whose information lives in diagrams are out of scope.

Prove and train on the corpus. Setup: Goedel-Prover v2 (8B) Pass@1 on all 177,597 problems; SFT on successful traces from one attempt per problem, or DPO on (success, failure) pairs from two attempts (7,148 pairs); 8 A100s, one epoch. Result: base 13.6% (two runs 13.62 and 13.58%), SFT 15.1%, DPO 15.0%; paired gain / loss counts 5,635 / 2,988 (SFT) and 5,338 / 2,853 (DPO).

Check held-out problems and a second prover. Setup: OMNI-Geometry, never used in training; DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B fine-tuned on its own successful proofs from a random half of Numina-Geometry for two epochs. Result: OMNI-Geometry Pass@1 6.90% base, 7.68% SFT, 7.81% DPO (Pass@2 8.33, 9.11, 8.59%); DeepSeek-Prover-V2 13.4% to 15.0% on the same half-corpus.

Note the in-distribution evaluation. Setup: the main Pass@1 is measured on the same corpus whose solved problems supplied the training traces (and DeepSeek-Prover-V2 is evaluated on the half it trained on), so part of the gain can come from re-solving trained problems; the held-out gain is under 1 point. Proved statements may also be misformalised (e.g. trivially true from over-strong hypotheses), so proof rate does not by itself certify faithfulness. Each gain is from one training run.
